ideas.hypothesis: In multinational clinical trials, the test-retest reliability of translated quality-of-life instruments varies more across language versions than internal consistency does. Language versions with lower test-retest reliability yield lower responsiveness, and so smaller estimated treatment effects, at the sites where they are used.
ideas.test: Secondary analysis of a multinational trial (or pooled trials) that gave the WHOQOL-BREF or a similar instrument twice during a stable run-in period and again after treatment, across at least four language versions. Compute the ICC and Cronbach's alpha for each language version, and the standardized response mean in the treatment arm. Then relate site-level responsiveness to the ICC and to alpha in a mixed model.
ideas.disconfirming: Test-retest ICCs are similar across language versions, or they do not predict site-level responsiveness any better than Cronbach's alpha.

ideas.hypothesis: When SF-36 versions are adapted across cultures, role-functioning subscales show weaker convergent validity in non-Western samples. Subscale-level convergent validity predicts responsiveness in clinical trials better than internal consistency does.
ideas.test: Pool longitudinal trial or cohort datasets from three or more countries that include the SF-36 and a reference measure (e.g., GHQ-28 or a disease-specific instrument) before and after an intervention. For each subscale and country, compute the convergent correlation, Cronbach's alpha and the standardized response mean. Regress responsiveness on convergent validity and alpha together.
ideas.disconfirming: Alpha predicts responsiveness as well as or better than convergent validity does, or role subscales show no weaker convergent validity in non-Western samples.

ideas.hypothesis: Service industries most exposed to globally fragmented, digitally mediated value chains are disproportionately those whose outputs are hardest to measure with constant-quality prices. As a result, the measured productivity slowdown in services is concentrated in these industries, which makes them the top priority for price-measurement research.
ideas.test: Code NAICS service industries by Diewert-style difficulty of price measurement. Merge with BEA input-output data on imported intermediate services and IT capital intensity, and with BLS/BEA industry productivity growth for 1987-2007. Regress the change in productivity growth on measurement difficulty interacted with offshoring and digital intensity.
ideas.disconfirming: Measurement difficulty is unrelated to offshoring or digital exposure, or hard-to-measure industries show no larger measured productivity slowdown.

ideas.hypothesis: As in prostate cancer, lung cancer patients enrolled in clinical trials do not generate higher costs for the public payer than comparable patients on standard care. Trial participation is also associated with less economic hardship one year after diagnosis, especially for minority patients, which weakens the case that trials are a cost burden on research funding.
ideas.test: Use a lung cancer cohort with survey follow-up (CanCORS-type) linked to Medicare or payer claims. Identify trial participants and match them to eligible non-participants by stage, age, comorbidity and race. Compare 12-month payer costs using standardized price templates, and economic hardship at 12 months, including interactions with race/ethnicity.
ideas.disconfirming: Trial participants have significantly higher payer costs, or report equal or greater economic hardship, than matched standard-care patients.

ideas.hypothesis: Longer commutes crowd out time spent on active recreation (walking, exercise, sports), and the crowd-out is stronger in winter months and colder climate regions, where the remaining daylight and weather leave fewer substitutes.
ideas.test: Use pooled ATUS diaries from 2003-2019 for employed respondents on workdays, measuring commuting consistently as proposed in the ATUS commuting method. Regress minutes of active recreation on commute minutes interacted with month and climate region, with sociodemographic controls and a Tobit or two-part specification.
ideas.disconfirming: Commute time is unrelated to active recreation, or the relationship is the same across seasons and climate regions.

ideas.hypothesis: In cost-utility studies that derive utilities from the SF-36 via the SF-6D, the choice of national preference value set and the handling of missing quality-of-life data due to death shift cost-per-QALY estimates across common reimbursement thresholds. The missing-data choice has the larger effect in palliative cohorts.
ideas.test: Re-analyse a cancer cohort with repeated SF-36 and cost data (e.g., resected versus palliative pancreatic cancer). Compute QALYs using two or more national SF-6D tariffs, and under complete-case analysis, multiple imputation, and death coded as zero utility. Compare the ICERs and the share of bootstrap replicates below a threshold.
ideas.disconfirming: The ICERs and threshold decisions are robust across tariffs and missing-data methods.

ideas.hypothesis: Steps to deepen the European Research Area (moving from FP6 to FP7) increased cross-border collaboration in EU transport research and reduced fragmentation. The rise is concentrated among institutions in newer member states.
ideas.test: Use CORDIS project participation data for transport projects in FP5-FP7, plus bibliometric co-authorship for EU transport researchers over 1998-2015. Run difference-in-differences comparing cross-border collaboration shares for EU institutions with a benchmark such as US/Canadian cross-institution collaboration, split by old and new member states.
ideas.disconfirming: Cross-border collaboration shares do not rise relative to the benchmark, or the rise is no greater for new member states.

ideas.hypothesis: Allocation of EU Framework Programme funding across surface-transport research topics is weakly proportional to the social burden each topic addresses (fatalities, emissions, congestion costs). This is the kind of misalignment that justice-based approaches to setting research priorities would flag.
ideas.test: Classify FP6 and FP7 surface-transport projects by topic using CORDIS. Sum EU contributions per topic and pair them with EU-level burden indicators (road deaths, transport CO2, estimated congestion costs). Estimate the elasticity of funding with respect to burden and compare across programme periods.
ideas.disconfirming: Funding is roughly proportional to burden (elasticity near one), or alignment improves markedly without explicit fairness criteria.

ideas.hypothesis: Trials that use quality-of-life instruments whose local-language versions were validated for responsiveness, and that analyse scores with methods suited to bounded, skewed scales, report more consistent treatment effects across studies than trials that rely only on reliability evidence and standard parametric tests.
ideas.test: Run a meta-research review of randomized trials using the Seattle Angina Questionnaire or SF-36 across countries. Code whether the local version had published responsiveness evidence and whether the statistical methods suited the score distribution. Compare between-study heterogeneity (I-squared) of treatment effects across these strata.
ideas.disconfirming: Heterogeneity is no lower among trials that use responsiveness-validated instruments and appropriate methods.

ideas.hypothesis: Research agenda items on the effects of digital technologies (e-commerce, telecommunications and travel) that specify concrete data needs are more likely to be taken up by later published research than items framed only conceptually.
ideas.test: Code each agenda item from the 2001-2002 transportation workshop reports as data-specified or conceptual. Count peer-reviewed papers addressing each item over 2002-2015 using standardized keyword searches with two independent coders. Compare uptake rates with a count model.
ideas.disconfirming: Uptake rates for data-specified items are no higher than for conceptual items.
